messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

Project brief: Two-stage rocket with an O-class booster and an M-class sustainer. Minimum apogee is 7,500 m. All parts should come down under 18 ft/s. It usually blows around 4 m/s at our field. The launch site is at 1,300 m elevation.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Two stages. The booster is O class and the sustainer is M class, both fixed as classes rather than one designation. Apogee is a minimum of 7,500 m. Every part lands under 18 ft/s: 18 * 0.3048 = 5.49 m/s. Wind is 4 m/s, stated, not the 2 m/s default. The site is at 1,300 m elevation, so that goes on the simulation too. Rail length is not stated, so 1.5 m. Drag-free speed for 7,500 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 7500) = 384 m/s.
2. Feasibility: An O booster plus an M sustainer is tens of thousands of newton-seconds, so 7,500 m is plausible if the stack is not a barn. The hard part is getting both pieces under 5.49 m/s, which means a real canopy on each stage, and passing 4 m/s wind plus the 1,300 m site. I need one O and one M from the catalog, with diameters that can stack.

2. Feasibility: The booster is Cesaroni 21062O3400-P, class O, 21041 N*s, 3421 N average, 98 mm by 1.239 m, 16.842 kg. The sustainer is AeroTech M1297W, class M, 5413.8 N*s, 1275 N, 75 mm by 0.665 m, 4.637 kg. The M1939W came back as class N, so it does not count. Both motors only list a 0 s delay, so both chutes are electronic. Together that is about 26,500 N*s. On a guessed 28 kg stack, liftoff thrust-to-weight is 3421 / (28 * 9.81) = 12.5, and 7,500 m is a reasonable ask rather than a fantasy.
3. Size: Booster empty is about 28 - 11 = 17 kg of which the sustainer leaves, so the booster section itself is near 17 - 7 = 10 kg after the split. Call the falling booster 9.7 kg and the sustainer 3.9 kg. At 5 m/s, the booster needs 2 * 9.7 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 7.8 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 7.8 / 3.1416) = 3.2 m. The sustainer needs 2 * 3.9 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 3.1 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 3.1 / 3.1416) = 2.0 m. I will use 3.4 m and 2.2 m so both stay under 5.49 m/s. The O case is 0.098 m, so the shared tube is 0.110 m and the booster mount is 0.102 m.
4. Draft: Sustainer on top: fiberglass ogive 0.35 m, 1.0 m tube, M1297W plugged in a 0.080 m mount, 2.2 m chute at apogee, smaller fins (root 0.22 m, span 0.14 m). Booster below, separates at burnout, 1.55 m tube, O3400 plugged in a 0.102 m by 1.28 m mount, 3.4 m chute at apogee, fins root 0.32 m, tip 0.12 m, span 0.22 m, sweep 0.16 m, 6 mm fiberglass. Both tubes 0.110 m, wall 3 mm. Wind 4 m/s and site 1,300 m on the run.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: The simulator gives 3259.2 m at 7.64 s, far under the 7,500 m minimum, and the sustainer never deploys (still at 684.6 m/s when the branch ends). Rail-exit margin is 0.97 cal, under 1.0, and the burn minimum is 0.35 cal. The booster does recover: 5.3 m/s under its chute. Rail exit speed 20.5 m/s and thrust-to-weight 11.3 pass. Mass is 30.8 kg. The stack is pitching over at the end of the O burn instead of handing a straight sustainer to the M.
5. Fix: The failing value behind the low apogee is 0.97 cal. Upper fins are pulling CP forward on a tail-heavy O. I am cutting the sustainer fins to root 0.16 m and span 0.10 m, and growing the booster fins to root 0.40 m, tip 0.16 m, span 0.30 m, sweep 0.18 m. Motors, chutes, tubes, 4 m/s wind, and the 1,300 m site stay the same.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: Bigger fins made the rail margin 2.92 cal, then the burn minimum went to -0.32 cal. Apogee is 2524.2 m at 6.68 s, still the end of the booster burn, and the sustainer again never deploys. The booster lands at 5.6 m/s, just over the 5.49 m/s cap. Rail exit 20.0 m/s and thrust-to-weight 11.0 still pass. Mass 31.7 kg. About 11 kg of O propellant is a third of the rocket, so the CG sprints forward during the burn and the 2.92 cal head start is gone before separation.
5. Fix: The failing number is -0.32 cal, and 2524.2 m is what that tumble produces. I am bolting 8 kg into the booster at 1.3 m from the top of its tube, down by the motor, so the propellant is a smaller share of the tail mass and the CG does not walk as far. The booster chute grows from 3.4 m to 3.8 m because 5.6 m/s missed 5.49 m/s. Fins and motors stay. Wind 4 m/s, site 1,300 m.

4. Check: The burn stays positive now, 0.39 cal, and the rail is 1.54 cal, so the booster itself is legal. The flight still dies at 7.04 s with apogee 2224 m, and the sustainer never deploys. I cut its fins too far. The booster, now carrying 8 kg of ballast, lands at 6.4 m/s, over 5.49 m/s. Rail exit 17.9 m/s and thrust-to-weight 8.8 pass. Mass 39.8 kg.
5. Fix: The failing flight is the sustainer, apogee 2224 m with no recovery. Its fins go back up to root 0.24 m, tip 0.09 m, span 0.16 m, sweep 0.11 m, so the M has a chance after separation. Booster fins grow with them, span 0.30 m to 0.34 m and root 0.40 m to 0.44 m, to keep the stack above 1 cal. The booster chute goes to 5.0 m because 6.4 m/s missed 5.49 m/s once the ballast was aboard. Last pass. Wind 4 m/s, site 1,300 m.
